(MarijuanaNews note: I delayed posting this story because I wanted to see how it was covered and also I wanted to be able to give it a little thought. My travel schedule has made that more difficult!

In the meantime, the media swamped the NORML office with calls, and one network even sent a camera crew promoting this story, after largely ignoring the report on marijuana ingredients helping MS symptoms.

The notion that marijuana use might trigger a heart attack in those with pre-existing conditions is at least plausible, in that THC increases the heart rate in some users. However, I am very uncomfortable with this report.

First, it appears that this work has not been published in a reputable medical journal, which means that there has been no " peer review. " A lot of garbage gets published, but that should have been a caution to the media.
See

There Are None So Blind As Ophthalmologists Who Don’t Want to See:
Marijuana, Glaucoma, Science And Journalism -- Analysis -- And 3 News Articles

Second, we do not really know how many marijuana users there are – of any age – so whether marijuana users are more – or less -- likely to have a heart attack cannot be readily determined. For example, there are so many marijuana users that, if some did not have heart attacks after smoking, one might infer that marijuana actually prevents heart attacks. That is actually possible inasmuch as marijuana use reduces stress, which is a recognized health risk. In any case, correlation is not causality.

Third, one of the most overlooked confounding factors in such studies is that much marijuana use, particularly by older users, may be palliative, so -- if person was not feeling well as the result of a heart problem -- marijuana might be used in an attempt at self-medication. In that case, the onset of the heart condition actually would have caused the marijuana use, not the other way around.

Fourth, it is clear that based on the numbers presented, the risk – if it exists – is very small. Less than 50 in a million.

Finally, if they are so concerned about our health, when is the medical profession going to do a study on the health effects of being arrested? The continued failure to study this wide-spread problem is both bad science and bad medicine.)

March 2, 2000

Aging pot users at risk for heart attack

SAN DIEGO, Mar 02 (Reuters Health) -- Aging marijuana smokers have almost a five times higher than normal risk of having a heart attack in the first hour after smoking cannabis, according to findings presented at the American Heart Association's 40th Annual Conference on Cardiovascular Disease Epidemiology and Prevention.

" To my knowledge, this is the first study to document that smoking marijuana can trigger a heart attack,'' said researcher Dr. Murray A. Mittleman of Beth Israel-Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, Massachusetts.

Mittleman and colleagues collected data from 3,882 persons who were treated for heart attacks at 62 participating medical centers over an 8-year period. A third of this group of patients were women, and their ages ranged from 20 to 92.

At a press conference, Mittleman said the researchers concentrated on ``any possible contributing factor during the days and weeks leading up to the heart attack.''

" There was a 4.8-fold increase in the relative risk of heart attack during the first hour after smoking marijuana,''

Mittleman said in an interview with Reuters Health. But he also noted that this increased risk drops rapidly, returning to normal after a few hours.

" This indicates a rapid decline in the dangerous effects of marijuana on the heart, but the short-term risk is considerable, especially for patients with other risk factors,'' said the researcher in a statement.

Mittleman said 124, or 3.2%, of the heart attack survivors in the study said they were regular marijuana users, and 37 said they had used marijuana within 24 hours of having a heart attack. Additionally, nine patients said they smoked marijuana within an hour of symptom onset.

The demographics of the marijuana users differed from the 3,758 non-users in that they were younger, average age 43 compared with 62, and were less likely to have the heart risk factors high blood pressure, diabetes or a history of angina (chest pain). However, they were twice as likely to be tobacco smokers and much more likely to be obese. ``Marijuana smokers were also more sedentary,'' said Mittleman.

Twenty-two of the 124 marijuana users were daily users, 30 used it at least once a week, 32 used it a few times a month and 40 used marijuana less than once a month, Mittleman said.

But it is not clear whether it is marijuana itself or compounds found in smoke, such as carbon monoxide, that increase the risk.

Mittleman noted that marijuana appears to pose less of a risk to the heart than cocaine, which causes much sharper rises in heart rate and blood pressure. But because marijuana use is more widespread, the overall threat to public health may be even greater than that from cocaine.
(MarijuanaNews note: This is simply prohibitionist propaganda. Over-the-counter drugs kill more people than cocaine.)

The findings also provide ``possible new food for thought'' in the continuing debate over the medical use of marijuana, Mittleman noted.
(MarijuanaNews note: Why? When one consider the risk in other medications, the risk in using medical marijuana would be very small by comparison.)

March 3, 2000

Study: Marijuana Raises Heart Risks

By DANIEL Q. HANEY AP Medical Editor


SAN DIEGO (AP) - Boomers pushing into their 50s probably should add another item to their list of things to worry about: The effect of marijuana on their hearts.

A study released Thursday documents for the first time that smoking pot increases the risk of a heart attack.

The chance of keeling over from a single joint is tiny, just as no one dies from one cigarette. But the cumulative effect on large numbers of 1960s children taking their pot habit into middle age could be significant.

" With baby boomers aging, more people in (their) 40s and 50s are smoking marijuana than in prior generations,'' said Dr. Murray Mittleman of the Harvard School of Public Health and Boston's Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center. ``The risk of coronary artery disease increases with age. Whether this will emerge as a public health problem remains to be seen.''

Mittleman presented the data at a conference in San Diego of the American Heart Association.

The study found that the risk of a heart attack is five times higher than usual in the hour after smoking a joint.

To put this into perspective, many things can trigger a heart attack, including just climbing out of bed in the morning. The researchers said that for someone in good shape, marijuana is about twice as risky as exercising or having sex.

The researchers questioned 3,882 heart attack victims - men and women - at 62 locations across the country about their habits and found that 124 were marijuana users. While pot was uncommon among the elderly heart patients, 13 percent of those under age 50 said they smoke it.

Among those questioned, 37 had their heart attacks within a day of using marijuana, including nine within an hour afterward.

The researchers calculated that someone's risk of a heart attack is five times higher during the hour after using marijuana. After an hour, the risk falls to twice normal. It soon returns to the usual level.

Whether a fivefold increase is a worry depends on whether someone has other risk factors, such as high blood pressure or diabetes. The increased risk is probably insignificant for a 20-year-old, whose chance of a heart attack is vanishingly small anyway.

" With baby boomers aging, more people in 40s and 50s are smoking marijuana than in prior generations,'' Mittleman said. " The risk of coronary artery disease increases with age. Whether this will emerge as a public health problem remains to be seen.''

(MarijuanaNews note: The fact that only a tiny number of heart attacks MAY have been triggered by marijuana use does not indicate any sort of " public health problem " – even if the study’s conclusions are valid.)
In any case, the risk of a heart attack from any single session of marijuana smoking is likely to be low. Mittleman said that for an otherwise healthy 50-year-old man, it is about 10 in 1 million.

Marijuana typically makes the heart speed up by about 40 beats a minute. Whether this is how it contributes to heart attacks is unclear. Mittleman noted that while marijuana doesn't contain nicotine, the smoke is otherwise similar to cigarette smoke.
(MarijuanaNews note: Not all marijuana users experience such an increase.)
In general, the marijuana smokers in the study were more likely than other heart attack victims to be overweight and sedentary, but they were less apt to have diabetes, high blood pressure or badly clogged arteries.

" My advice on marijuana is, `Don't,''' said Dr. Lynn Smaha of Sayre, Pa., president of the heart association. ``If they have heart disease, I'd tell patients they are playing a dangerous game if they smoke marijuana.''
(MarijuanaNews note: On the basis of the numbers presented here, the risk would appear to be a little less than 50 in a million for someone with heart disease. If the risk is 10 in a million for someone with no heart problems, and it is 4.8 times greater with heart disease, then it would be 48 in a million with heart disease. What kind of " dangerous game " is that? How does that compare with the risks in using other substances and other activities?)

Mittleman said the possibility of triggering a heart attack should be considered when deciding whether to smoke marijuana for medicinal purposes such as to relieve the nausea of chemotherapy.

(MarijuanaNews note: In other words, the patient would have less of a risk of a heart attack from violent vomiting than from taking two hits on a joint? I don’t think so. Also not using marijuana might cause the patient to lose weight and even drop out of chemotherapy. This is really a wretched comment that causes me to doubt his judgement and objectivity.)
